newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland Bank seen intervening amid ERM talk.
newsitem.headline: Finland Bank seen intervening amid ERM talk.

text.p: The Bank of Finland intervened on markets on Tuesday, selling markka for German marks amid mounting speculation that new member Finland may decide this weekend to link its currency to the European Union's stability mechanism, dealers said.

"The Bank of Finland has been selling markka for marks," one senior currency dealer said. A central bank official, in line with usual policy, declined comment. The Bank has a stated policy of acting to curb sudden, sharp moves in the markka.

The markka on Monday was sharply boosted by comments from Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen that the time was ripe for a decision in the near future on a link between the markka and the ERM -- the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Lipponen also said no manipulation of the exchange rate would be possible before a link is established.
Dealers said the intervention suggested the central bank was aiming to curb strength in the currency ahead of any link.
This could peg the Finnish currency at a rate which may damage the interests of exporters in forestry and engineering.
"There are many, including the Bank of Finland, who think the markka has been too strong -- ahead of a possible ERM link," said another dealer.
But the central bank's activity failed to turn a rising trend in the Finnish currency, which closed at a four-week high of 2.9975 against the German mark.
The Finnish government has repeatedly said a key objective is to ensure Finland can be among the first countries to join the EU's single curremcy due in 1999.
A recently updated convergence programme for monetary union showed Finland will in 1997 meet most other criteria for joining.
But most experts -- among them German Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer -- say membership of the ERM is also key to fulfil the exchange rate stability criterion for convergence.
His comments have prompted Finnish exporters to convert foreign currency earnings amid mounting concerns that the markka may strengthen more ahead of any link to ERM, dealers said.

Ruling Finnish politicians are seeking tight links with the EU as part of a bid to ensure closer political connections with the west for Finland, which joined the Union in 1995 after 50 years in the shadow of the former Soviet Union.
They are anxious to ensure that if monetary union is acheived on schedule, Finland will not be excluded because of a technicality like ERM membership.
Some analysts said the right time to link the markka could be in connection with the coming weekend's meeting of EU finance and economy ministers in Dublin.
But dealers also said the markka was also tracking the firmer Swedish crown and French franc.

Others, including Finnish exporters, fear the markka is too strong and a link now may jeopardise Finland's competitive position, particularly against its main forestry rival, Sweden which has not yet decided on whether to join a single currency

The central bank itself has also voiced concern that a link may paradoxically make the recently stable markka more volatile, by inviting speculators to challenge the fluctuation limits imposed by membership of the ERM.
Dealers said the markka was expected to turn more volatile towards the end of the week as overseas players were likely to join the ERM-linked speculative trading.
